questions.problem: Find the surface area of the part of the surface $y=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{z}^{2}}$ whose projection onto the $xz$-plane  is bounded by the constraints $-1\le x\le 1$ and $1\le z\le 2.$
questions.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $y=f(x,z)$ with $(x,z)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂y}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂y}{∂z})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

In this case, our surface is given by

$$
y=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{z}^{2}},\,(x,z)\in D,
$$

where 

$$
D=\{(x,z)\,:\,-1\le x\le 1,\,1\le z\le 2\},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14274587/assets/06abf7781e46ea3d3434ee26c6711cea2930fa8f73d534d6622931bf3c47c6a6.png)

Now, since

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂y}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{z}^{2}})=\frac{x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{z}^{2}}}, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{z}^{2}})=\frac{z}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{z}^{2}}},\end{aligned}
$$

the surface area is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂y}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂y}{∂z})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{z}^{2}}})}^{2}+{(\frac{z}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{z}^{2}}})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+\frac{{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{z}^{2}}+\frac{{z}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{z}^{2}}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{\frac{2({x}^{2}+{z}^{2})}{{x}^{2}+{z}^{2}}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & =\sqrt{2}{∬}_{D}\,\text{d}A \\  & =\sqrt{2}\cdot \text{Area}(D) \\  & =\sqrt{2}\cdot (1-(-1))\cdot (2-1) \\  & =2\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14274587/assets/0ea0204d3e1f230efcde4b82da36b1986af732cdf2a01ad868aa0f6bf7414326.png)

Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)=4y\,i+(2x-1)\,j$ through the curve $C$ given by $r(t)={t}^{2}\,i+t\,j$ for $t\in [0,1],$ measured with respect to the unit normal vector $n$ on $C,$ as shown above.
questions.worked_solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ measured with respect to a unit normal vector $n$ on $C$ is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x.
$$

To apply this formula, 

- the curve should be parameterized as $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ and

- the unit normal vector $n$ *must* be a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of the unit tangent vector $T(t).$

In this case, $n$ is indeed a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of $T,$ so we can apply the above formula. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14274587/assets/59e503e0c4d950f030891bbaeb7ed890426ef470a1e1dae89d27eabb8dd591a6.png)

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x={t}^{2},\,y=t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =4y=4t, \\ Q(x,y) & =2x-1=2{t}^{2}-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})=2t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(4t)\cdot (1)-(2{t}^{2}-1)\cdot (2t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}4t-4{t}^{3}+2t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}6t-4{t}^{3}\,\text{d}t \\  & =3{t}^{2}-{t}^{4}{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(3-1)-(0-0){|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Given that

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{t}^{n}\} & =\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}, &  & s>0,\end{aligned}
$$

use linearity of Laplace transforms and the first shifting theorem to find the Laplace transform of $f(t)=5{t}^{2}+9t{e}^{3t}$ for $s>3.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we apply the linearity properties of Laplace transforms:

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{f(t)\} & =L\{5{t}^{2}+9t{e}^{3t}\} \\  & =L\{5{t}^{2}\}+L\{9t{e}^{3t}\} \\  & =5L\{{t}^{2}\}+9L\{t{e}^{3t}\}\end{aligned}
$$

We are given that, for $s>0,$

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{t}^{n}\} & =\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{t\} & =\frac{1}{{s}^{2}} \\ L\{{t}^{2}\} & =\frac{2}{{s}^{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

The first shifting theorem states that if $L\{f(t)\}=F(s),$ then $L\{{e}^{at}f(t)\}=F(s-a).$ Therefore,

$$
L\{t{e}^{3t}\}=\frac{1}{(s-3)^{2}}.
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $f(t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{f(t)\} & =5L\{{t}^{2}\}+9L\{t{e}^{3t}\} \\  & =5\cdot \frac{2}{{s}^{3}}+9\cdot \frac{1}{(s-3)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{10}{{s}^{3}}+\frac{9}{(s-3)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

This transform is valid for $s>3.$

Let $V={R}_{2}[t],$ the vector space of real polynomials of degree at most $2,$ and let the inner product on $V$ be defined as

$$
⟨p(t),q(t)⟩=p(-1)q(-1)+p(0)q(0)+p(1)q(1).
$$

Now consider the following elements of $V:$

$$
{p}_{1}(t)={t}^{2}-t,\,{p}_{2}(t)={t}^{2}+t,\,q(t)=4{t}^{2}-t-1
$$

Find the orthogonal projection of $q(t)$ onto $S=\text{Span}\{{p}_{1}(t),{p}_{2}(t)\}$ given that ${p}_{1}(t)⊥{p}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the inner product, and that the orthogonal projection of $q(t)$ onto $\text{Span}\{{p}_{1}(t)\}$ equals $2{t}^{2}-2t.$

questions.problem: What surface is defined by the equation ${z}^{2}=2{r}^{2}$ in cylindrical polar coordinates?
questions.worked_solution:
The position of a point in cylindrical polar coordinates is written as $(r,\theta ,z),$ where 

- $r\ge 0$ and $\theta \in [0,2\pi )$ are the usual plane polar coordinates, and

- $z\in (-\infty ,\infty )$ is the usual Cartesian $z$-coordinate.

With that in mind, let's examine our equation:

$$
{z}^{2}=2{r}^{2}
$$

This equation requires that the square of the distance from any point on the surface to the $xy$-plane equals twice the square of the distance from that point to the $z$-axis. In other words, the tangent of the angle between any position vector on the surface and the $z$-axis must be equal to

$$
\frac{r}{z}=\sqrt{\frac{{r}^{2}}{{z}^{2}}}=\pm \sqrt{\frac{{r}^{2}}{2{r}^{2}}}=\pm \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}.
$$

Since the tangent of this angle can be a positive or negative number, the $z$-coordinate can also be positive or negative.

On the other hand, $\theta $ can vary arbitrarily in its domain. 

Therefore, our surface is the cone shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14274587/assets/7c8d0cefa5eb8da76f6cba59570670e4078c278c801aeb12344dce3183733149.png)
